about.heading: Level 0.5
about.introParagraph: There are spaces that feel almost familiar, but never fully arrive—half-floors, loading rooms, empty corridors, fluorescent lights, office carpets, abandoned malls, and repeated architecture that seem to exist between function and disappearance. Level 0.5 is not a destination, but a threshold: the space between systems, the room before an image fully renders, the hallway after a memory begins to fade. Rather than treating the unknown space only as a horror setting, this exhibition asks what happens when comfort turns strange, and when familiar environments begin to glitch, loop, or slowly detach from us.
pressParagraphs: New York, NY — A Space Virtual Gallery is pleased to present Level 0.5, a group exhibition in virtual space that gathers artists responding to the feeling of being caught between arrival and disappearance. The show brings together works across painting, sculpture, video, print, drawing, zine, photography, and digital media, moving through liminal space, digital loneliness, architectural anxiety, simulation, memory, nostalgia, repetition, and the quiet unease of being suspended inside a place without a clear exit.

The exhibition explores the blurred boundary between the real and the artificial, the physical and the virtual, comfort and fear, orientation and loss. Rather than offering a way out, Level 0.5 creates space for wandering, suspension, disorientation, and quiet unease—for environments that resemble the ordinary but refuse to become complete.

Wade Kramm's Mirror Fragment (Corner) and Wall Fragment (Floor/Wall) extract familiar architectural corners from drywall, floorboards, and moulding, collapsing the distinction between object and reflection until the room itself becomes suspect. Nathalie Slowak's paired Untitled ink drawings depict interiors emptied of any figure, spaces detached from time and context that hover between memory and imagined countryside. Tommasino Maderna's sMTHng_fr((omt))hehe@@RT renders five secret sentences from friends as a ray-marched black form suspended in pale space, where intimacy survives precisely through what cannot be shared.

Wu Chen's Always Becoming, Never Arriving loops through a mirrored revolving door where the viewer is both subject and object of an infinite passage. Sibyl Guo's we are here drifts down a backroom corridor of repeating wooden frames as a seed grows into a Tyrannosaurus skull. Tianyu Zhang's This game finds you in the 2000s stitches together shifting dream-rooms into a video game that will not let you go home. Théo Arnaudet's Level 0, Level 3 and Level 37 (3 Zines) builds a personal mythology of half-floors through riso-printed pages, while Sogen assembles Yu-Gi-Oh!-inspired landscapes and Charente limestone into an installation caught between digital myth and regional geology.

Kristóf Lázár's Kill Mr. Yuk and Fuck Mr. Ouch treat advertising mascots as contemporary golems, animated by collective belief and internet repetition into new cultural archetypes. Paule Cerdá Llorente's LEVEL ⬮: THE ANGEL NEST unsettles a familiar room with the burrow of a genderless angel, reclaiming a female experience through a figure that exists beyond the binary. Andrew Wharton's Chimera (Edison) and Chimera (Monkeyshines) pass early cinema through a custom deer-trained diffusion model, letting archival human figures dissolve into shifting animal-machine hybrids. Freja Jiahui Ye's Damp Town and Amor Fati hold their own weathered atmospheres of loop and lull.

Queenie Si's photographs The Great Wall and Balloons tell fortunes through fragments of a self on the edge of becoming. Mengwei Chen's Visitant and Ghost in the Shell flicker between paper-cut absence and holographic presence, mourning home as it slips from lived place into virtual nostalgia. Rudi Jie-A-Fa's mixed-media drawings Story Time: I Found a Sword On the Ground and Accidentally Turned a Guy into Stone and Mind Palace I narrate small, isolated protagonists inside chaotic dark seas of markmaking. Vivi Walsh's Recommended by pinterest and Shot reconstruct degraded internet-era images and outdated mall interiors as artifacts of a memory that keeps mutating.
Together, the works do not resolve the strangeness of these in-between spaces. They stay inside the glitch, the loop, the fluorescent hum—making room for the quiet freedom of not quite arriving.

currentShow.title: Mirror Fragment (Corner)
currentShow.description: This work presents a familiar architectural corner that appears to occupy the surface of a mirror. Constructed from drywall, floorboards, and moulding, the reflected corner is not an image but a fabricated fragment of architecture relocated into the frame. The work disrupts the expected relationship between object and reflection, collapsing distinctions between physical space and representation. What initially reads as a conventional mirror gradually reveals itself as a material intervention, prompting viewers to reconsider how they orient themselves within the surrounding environment. Familiar space becomes subtly unstable, drawing attention to the processes through which perception constructs experience.

currentShow.title: Wall Fragment (Floor/Wall)
currentShow.medium: Drywall, floorboards, moulding, and house paint.
currentShow.description: Constructed from the same drywall, floorboards, and moulding as the architecture it occupies, this work isolates and reconfigures a familiar corner into a self contained fragment. Removed from the continuity of the wall and floor, the materials no longer function as architecture but as an autonomous object that nevertheless remains visually inseparable from its surroundings. The work occupies a threshold between sculpture and built environment, prompting viewers to question where the architecture ends and the artwork begins. Through careful replication and precise fabrication, an ordinary spatial condition becomes subtly estranged, revealing how perception relies on assumptions of continuity, context, and material familiarity.

currentShow.title: sMTHng_fr((omt))hehe@@RT
currentShow.description: sMTHng_fr((omt))he:he@@RT is a single-channel audiovisual work built from five secret sentences entrusted to me by five friends. These sentences are never revealed to the viewer. Instead, they remain inaccessible, functioning as hidden emotional cores that generate the work without ever becoming fully legible. Each sentence was processed through a custom system that translated its linguistic and structural features into movement, giving rise to a shifting black form rendered through ray-marching. Suspended in a pale, undefined space, this viscous blob behaves like a living residue of language: unstable, intimate, and opaque. What appears on screen is not the confession itself, but its transformation into a visual body. The work reflects on language as both revelation and concealment, and on the way intimacy often survives precisely through what cannot be shared directly. By withholding the original text, sMTHng_fr((omt))he:he@@RT preserves the secrecy of each confession while allowing its emotional force to persist in another form. The piece becomes a meditation on trust, interiority, and the fragile passage through which private thought turns into image, movement, and presence.

currentShow.title: Always Becoming, Never Arriving
currentShow.description: This video documents a proposed spatial installation exploring thresholds, entering and exiting, self-observation, entrapment, and endless repetition. The revolving door functions as both a transitional device and a liminal space, becoming a site where bodily experience reveals underlying structures. More than a physical boundary, the revolving door represents a psychological condition suspended between movement and stagnation: one keeps moving but cannot truly stop, arrive, or enter. I often find myself looking toward a place that always seems just beyond reach. Once the revolving door is transformed into mirrored surfaces, visitors repeatedly encounter themselves as the surrounding environment constantly shifts, producing a continuous movement that never reaches resolution. The viewer becomes both subject and object. Moving through the installation destabilises one's sense of direction and identity while creating layered forms of observation: one is inside while being observed from outside, carried by the system while simultaneously witnessing oneself within it. The work also reflects on contemporary society through the idea of structured freedom—a condition in which escape remains possible, yet the available paths have already been designed. Freedom exists, but its routes are predetermined, leaving us suspended between absolute freedom and absolute control. Credits:Concept, Artistic Direction & Final Edit: Wu Chen, 3D Visualisation: Cristóbal Zepeda

currentShow.title: we are here
currentShow.description: In a backroom corridor filled with repeating wooden frames, a red metal box appears. A seed grows into a branch, bears fruit, and becomes a Tyrannosaurus rex skull. The red box recurs in my "Backrooms" series, a quiet signal from somewhere else. The strange light spectrum shifts from orange through blue to pale yellow, turning dread into something softer. The skull is not an ending, but a memory of an ancient encounter, a first attempt to take shape in a world that was never home. If you too are a being from elsewhere, you would recognize this feeling. Homesickness. Surprise. The quiet desperation of trying to belong where you cannot be seen. we are here is not a warning, but a fragile hope to exist somewhere that was never meant for you.

currentShow.title: Level 0, Level 3 and Level 37 (3 Zines)
currentShow.description: Since 2022, I have been developing a series of fanzines inspired by the mythology of the «backrooms». Rather than seeing it as a simple internet phenomenon, I approach it as a contemporary narrative model rooted in the aesthetics of liminal spaces: transitional, indeterminate environments that have become the setting for diffuse, collectively constructed stories. I use this framework as a field for experimentation, working within a set of simple constraints: a single space, an isolated character, and a fragmented narrative. Each publication follows a recurring format and a two-colour riso printing process, establishing an editorial continuity throughout the series. These stories function as self-contained fragments that can echo one another, resembling found or reconstructed narratives, much like the anonymous stories that circulate through online forums. Each volume explores different variations on these states of drifting and introspection. The first draws on the conventions of found footage; another imagines the formation of a closed group; while a third shifts these narrative structures towarda more personal territory, taking the limestonequarries and landscapes of the Poitou-Charentes region as its point of departure. Through this series, I am interested in how these narrative forms emerge, circulate, and evolve, and in what they reveal about the ways we produce and inhabit stories today. I would like to continue expanding this body of work by exploring more locally rooted myths, discovering them through artist residencies and integrating them into future publications.

currentShow.title: Sogen
currentShow.medium: Posters: Digital prints on non-woven polypropylene fabric banners, 100 × 50 cm. Labyrinth: Bonded plastic panels and limestone sculptures by Jonas Dauthuille, 100 × 50 × 10 cm.
currentShow.description: Sogen is an installation commissioned by CACA (Centre d'Art Contemporain d'Angoulême). It brings together landscapes inspired by the digital illustrations of the Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card game and a central labyrinth, evoking a sense of wandering between fiction and psychological space. Limestone sculptures from the Charente region, created by Jonas Dauthuille, anchor this imaginary world in a tangible local landscape, creating a dialogue between digital mythology and regional geology.

currentShow.title: This game finds you in the 2000s
currentShow.description: You wake up, dizzy, in a bathroom. You don't know why the walls and floor are shifting. You want to return to the home you know so well, but you can't find which door leads there. When you fall asleep again, even that familiar home has changed — you can no longer tell where reality ends and the dream begins. On the coffee table lies a blurred gun. In a corridor that doesn't exist in real life, you pick up the COVID-19 virus, and somehow it all feels so very far away. Beyond a strange room stretches another long hallway, where the childhood toy you always longed for and pages from your middle-school chemistry textbook loom impossibly large. At last, in the instant you leap off the bed, there is only a bottomless abyss. You wake up. There is no going back.The scenes in this work are reconstructed and stitched together from dreams I had at different ages. I hope viewers can find within it a sense of absurdity and nostalgia.

currentShow.title: Untitled
currentShow.description: The work depicts an interior space complete erased of any figures, showcasing an empty space deprived of any connections to time, location and context. Through scale, composition and the labor-intense technique of black mark-making, I am to create an intimate encounter that might convey a range of human emotions, from sorrow to devastation to serenity. The scene is of imaginary nature and the visual choices largely subconscious. However, my works refer to past experiences – there are traces of the summers spent in the Austrian countryside, a place where cycles of change can create a sense of timelessness.

currentShow.title: Kill Mr. Yuk
currentShow.description: This image is part of a series of three paintings entitled Fuck Mr. Ouch, Marry Mr. Clean, Kill Mr. Yuk. The three iconic figures, originally created for advertising, were brought together in a Twitter post as part of the “F Marry Kill” forced-choice game. The artistic reinterpretation of this post intrigued me on several levels. These characters no longer function merely as product mascots, detached from their original context, they take on an almost mythical quality within the circulation of online culture. Even seemingly mundane figures, such as the Michelin Man, acquire new significance when viewed through the metaphor of the golem, a legendary being formed from inanimate matter and brought to life through mystical means. Similarly, these figures become animated through collective belief and repetition, assuming a symbolic existence that extends beyond their commercial origins. The work reflects on the web as a contemporary site of myth-making, where familiar images inhabit a space between their original function and imagination, gradually transforming into shared cultural archetypes.

currentShow.title: LEVEL ⬮: THE ANGEL NEST
currentShow.description: This work invites the viewer to enter a dreamlike vision of the valley of the uncanny: a familiar room, yet deconstructed, where the burrow of an entity is found. It invites us into the nest of an angel. This profane space projects a personal perspective on otherness, understood through the feminine by means of a figure that exists beyond the binary. It explores how, in the separation between the “subject” as masculine and the “other” as belonging to femininity, woman is reduced to roles of care or to biological traits. Through a genderless figure, similar to an angel, a female experience such as pregnancy is embodied, reclaiming how existences outside binarism are structurally read. The other appears as a manifestation of the divine: an immaterial body made flesh, a transubstantiation of the word into that which does not beget. It also seeks to express how an unequal distribution of responsibilities produces structures that can give rise to unsafe childhoods. A metal nest houses the creature’s eggs; if you approach, it will appear. This is an audiovisual piece based on original sculptural elements as well as an animation and a sound art piece. It was originally conceived as an installation.

currentShow.title: Chimera (Edison)
currentShow.medium: Digital Video, Custom Image Diffusion LoRA, Archival Footage of Edison Pictures 'Frankenstein' 1910
currentShow.description: Chimera (Edison) is an experimental short film that reinterprets Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein through the lens of machine learning and archetypical myth. I trained a custom AI model on trail-camera images of deer and used it to transform Edison Picture’s 1910 Frankenstein, producing a shifting sequence of human–animal hybrids in a glitching forest environment. The film treats AI as a contemporary outcropping of technological folklore, where long-standing myths of artificial life re-emerge through algorithmic systems. By merging archival cinema, surveillance imagery, and generative hallucination, Chimera reflects on how data extraction, machine vision, and environmental observation reshape the boundary between human, animal, and machine intelligence. The work proposes the algorithm as a site of ritual and myth-making. An unstable space where new hybrid entities and speculative narratives can emerge.

currentShow.title: Chimera (Monkeyshines)
currentShow.medium: Digital Video, Custom Image Diffusion LoRA, Archival Footage from Edison Labs
currentShow.description: This pieces uses the Chimera Image Diffusion LoRA to reimagine 'Monkeyshines', an original film test used to test early Edison cameras. In the original footage, the ghostly figure of a human gestures vaguely against a solid black background. The model reinterprets this footage, occasionally able to parse and recreate the presence of a human. At other times, noise takes over and the model frantically produces amalgamations of deers, humans, and other spectres. This speaks to the process of capturing the image of human beings through different technologies, and the reflexive impact the particular contours of that technology have on our own image of ourselves as humans. This work is part of a series of five works, all using the same process to reinterpret diffent fragments of Edison's early film tests.

currentShow.title: Damp Town
currentShow.medium: Resin, Fossils, Hey, Latex, Metal, Stone, Fabric, The water of the River Thames, Marble, Leather, Animal bone, ceramic
currentShow.description: "Damp Town" is a site-responsive project that brings together sound, sculpture, and spatial installation as an eerie fictional town leaky with memories and animal presence. Dampness is understood as a living material that absorbs, stains, swells, decays, and reshapes space. It softens clear boundaries, disrupts order, and reveals what has been suppressed beneath the surface: residues, desires, unease, and hidden social vulnerabilities. A poignant horror in which fragments of bodies and relics haunt the space's wet walls, accompanied by the presence of footsteps, breathing, and heartbeats of the more-than-human. Skeletal structures and hybrid human forms are embedded in a surreal ambient soundscape, suspended between ruin and dream.

currentShow.title: Amor Fati
currentShow.description: Amor Fati: This performance work is inspired by the short story The Garden of Forking Paths.   It unfolds through craft, chemistry, and an alchemical process embedded with embodied temporality, transforming abstract philosophical speculations on parallel timelines into visual, sensory, and bodily experience. As time progresses and temperature differentials are rapidly manipulated, crystalline structures grow wildly across the surface of the textile through chemical processes, gradually reconfiguring into a wearable sculpture. The sharp edges of the crystals cut into the wearer’s skin, forcing every movement to become deliberate and tense. The body turns into a living labyrinth, where each posture carries the logic of temporal bifurcation, and every step unfolds within the possibility of irreversible consequences, saturating the space with a silent tension. The climax of the performance occurs when the figure submerges into a glass water tank, where the crystallised formations gradually dissolve back into water. (If the PDF quality is not sufficient due to compression, please feel free to contact me and I can send a higher-resolution version.) The Threshold of the Gaze: Who fired this bullet?: A hybrid humanoid creature reclines within a surreal environment surrounded by organic blue formations that resemble flames.       She is transformed into a hybrid creature, which disrupts the viewer’s conventional erotic mode of gazing. What first appears as a naked female body is reconfigured into something non-human, and potentially predatory, causing the gaze to lose its familiar structure of desire. A golden bullet violently ruptures the flat pictorial space, appearing to enter from an external three-dimensional world. The bullet is not a straightforward symbol of violence;       it is carrying traces of industrial design, phallic form, and object-like desirability, as a beautified intrusion in which violence is disguised as desire.

currentShow.title: The Great Wall
currentShow.description: This piece is part of the photography project The Eyes Become Mouths, The Mouths Become Eyes. This project was created when I became uncertain about who I was. Reality is constantly rearranging itself. Sleeping becomes exhausting. My dreams are too realistic. I get transported to a parallel universe where I live another day. My future started to blur. Shifting, shaking, always on the edge of becoming. I could no longer imagine what adulthood looked like.  I felt the nostalgia of myself. Once, in a subway station, a stranger stopped me. She told me two red lights were glowing above my head. She read my face. It felt like a diagnosis—for a creature I hadn't yet become. That encounter stayed with me. I started to tell fortunes through photographs. Not yet memories, nor truths. Fragments. Caught in the moment of becoming. Let us follow the trail. Hoping we can catch some glow.

currentShow.title: Visitant
currentShow.description: Visitant explores the gradual disappearance of home as a vessel of memory in the digital age. The work features a paper-cut figure with its body removed, leaving only a ghost-like outline and the trace of an absence. Beneath it, a house-shaped hologram flickers continuously, like a memory replaying itself without ever becoming fully accessible. As digital images increasingly occupy physical space, home shifts from a lived place into a form of virtual nostalgia—present, yet always out of reach. The work reflects on the unstable boundary between the physical and the virtual, presence and absence.

currentShow.title: Ghost in the Shell
currentShow.description: Ghost in the Shell depicts a girl living inside a giant snail shell. She appears to be telling a story, yet her voice can never be heard. The audience can only witness her silent presence through a holographic projection. The shell is both a refuge and a tomb. It offers protection while slowly isolating her from the outside world. The work reflects on the growing distance between the body, space, and digital imagery, and the loneliness of waiting for a response that never comes.

currentShow.title: Story Time: I Found a Sword On the Ground and Accidentally Turned a Guy into Stone
currentShow.description: In this artwork, I explore the idea of looking for an escape from guilt. A protagonist stares cutely and innocently at the viewer after fatally injuring a knight. They seem passively interested in the viewer while they hold the weapon, paying no mind while the knight turns to stone due to the cursed nature of the sword. Since the knight is no longer alive, the protagonist is alone with just the person watching the image. Even the mountains in the distance seem to be asleep, adding to the protagonists's sense of isolation. There seems to be no one else around, to answer the protagonist's question of what to do and how to get out. The border of snake-like coils does not close all the way, and one edge of the drawing lies open, offsetting any sense of visual safety or balance.

currentShow.title: Mind Palace I
currentShow.description: This artwork is a dark space that I have decorated with marks. I built up a dense and chaotic darkness by overlaying markmaking and tiny instances of color and drawings. A small child floats in the top corner of the dark ocean of marks, offering a "V for Victory" sign, an empty gesture amongst the chaos of the surrounding sea of shadows. Another child does the same while simply being passively engulfed by the chasm around him. The smaller drawings and collage elements make the darkness deeper, offset by layers of positive phrases, faces, and memories.

currentShow.title: Recommended by pinterest
currentShow.description: This was the second piece of a series based on some old digital collages I made when I was in high school. I was very into the "traumacore" visual aesthetic that was popular online at the time, and made some photo edits that went viral on places like Pinterest and Tumblr. Over time, these images escaped me and transformed into something else entirely. They suffered rounds of screenshotting, cropping, and reposting, becoming more degraded with each iteration. Years later, I tracked down as many variations as I could find, cut out parts of them, and rearranged them into new compositions. With this piece, I included other artifacts I found while reverse image searching the original hospital photo I used in the first collage from years ago, and generally let myself play around more with the composition of the painting as opposed to restricting myself to a more "faithful" recreation.

currentShow.title: Shot
currentShow.medium: Acrtlic and image transfer on canvas
currentShow.description: I've always been fascinated by slightly outdated interior and graphic design that have yet to be updated or replaced. To me, they act as artifacts of previous cultural values. I notice this phenomenon the most in malls and retail spaces. A few months ago, I started researching the local malls I went to growing up, and tracked down as many old photos, diagrams, and websites as I could. I came across one photo of a food court restaurant posted on a forgotten personal blog from 2011. The quality of the image strongly indicated to me that it was taken with one of the first iPhone models. "shot" is my way of recreating that feeling of seeing a photo taken using technology that was revolutionary for the time. When I was younger, I never expected phones to progress past the skeuomorphism era nor for that restaurant to close. I find that omitting key parts of the image and pixelating others to be a representation of memory and the cruel passage of time.
